name: Futakuchi-onna
description: Futakuchi-onna is a Japanese yokai — a two-mouthed woman — whose hair moves like serpents to feed a second, fully functional mouth on the back of her head that screams demands for food and causes excruciating pain if unfed.
full_description: The Futakuchi-onna (二口女, 'two-mouthed woman') is a Japanese yokai featuring a woman with two mouths — a normal one on her face and a second one on the back of the head, hidden beneath the hair. The second mouth is fully functional, with lips, teeth, and a tongue. The creature's hair moves independently like a pair of serpents, allowing it to manipulate food and feed the back mouth. If the second mouth is not fed, it causes the woman tremendous pain and screams constantly — mumbling spiteful and threatening things. The condition arises through a curse, with three primary origin narratives: (1) A wife of a miser eats little and develops a second mouth that demands food, consuming double what a normal person would eat; (2) A stingy woman struck in the head by her husband's axe while chopping wood develops an unhealable wound that transforms into the second mouth; (3) A stepmother or step-sibling who starves a child to death is possessed by the victim's spirit, which lodges in the body seeking revenge through the second mouth. The futakuchi-onna belongs to the same yokai category as rokurokubi, kuchisake-onna, and yama-uba — women afflicted with a curse or supernatural disease. It appears in the Ehon Hyaku Monogatari, an illustrated collection of ghost stories.
origin: A creature of Japanese folklore; associated with rural Japan in the Edo period and earlier. No specific geographic region within Japan is particularly associated with the futakuchi-onna.

etymology.origin: Japanese (ふたくちおんな / 二口女)
etymology.meaning: Futa (二, two) + kuchi (口, mouth) + onna (女, woman) = 'two-mouthed woman'
etymology.first_use: Edo period Japan; appears in the Ehon Hyaku Monogatari (illustrated ghost story collection)

timeline.event: Ehon Hyaku Monogatari published, containing an early illustrated account of the futakuchi-onna
timeline.significance: Earliest known illustrated documentation of the creature in print

related.name: Rokurokubi
related.description: Japanese yokai of a woman with an elongated or detachable neck; same category of female body-horror yokai

related.name: Kuchisake-onna
related.description: Japanese yokai / urban legend of a slit-mouthed woman; shares the mouth-horror motif

related.name: Yama-uba
related.description: Japanese mountain hag yokai; same category of supernatural woman cursed or transformed

cultural_notes: The futakuchi-onna embodies the belief that cruelty and greed — particularly within the domestic sphere — will be punished through supernatural means. The hidden mouth represents hidden sins becoming inescapably manifest.
